claims.text: The starting material is an equiatomic Ti–Zr–Hf–Mo–V alloy, corresponding to approximately 20 at.% of each element.
The equiatomic Ti–Zr–Hf–Mo–V alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
Incrementally replacing Mo with V increases atomic-size mismatch in Ti–Zr–Hf–Mo–V.
Greater atomic-size mismatch produces enhanced lattice distortion and local strain.
Keeping every constituent above 5 at.% during Mo-for-V substitution retains the single-phase solid solution.
Lattice distortion and local strain can be quantified using X-ray diffraction peak broadening and pair-distribution-function analysis.
Local strain caused by atomic-size mismatch alters phonon modes.
Changes in the phonon spectrum alter electron–phonon coupling.
Electron–phonon coupling controls Cooper pairing and therefore affects superconducting Tc within a BCS framework.
Lattice vibrational properties govern Tc in Ti–Zr–Hf–Mo–V.
Moderate V substitution has an optimum that raises Tc above the equiatomic-alloy baseline.
Excessive V substitution and lattice distortion lower Tc through enhanced electron scattering.
The expected dependence of Tc on V substitution and measured lattice distortion is non-monotonic.
Arc melting followed by homogenization annealing at approximately 1000 °C is the prescribed processing route.
The proposed mechanism is limited to ambient pressure, homogenized samples, and compositions for which electron-count changes are minimal.
Changing the Mo/V ratio may alter electron concentration and confound attribution of Tc changes to lattice distortion.
Electronic-structure measurements are needed to distinguish lattice-distortion effects from band-filling effects.

contradictions.description: The uncertainty field correctly treats a significant electron-count change as a confounder that prevents isolation of the lattice-distortion effect, whereas the falsification rule treats the same confounder as directly falsifying the mechanism. A confounded substitution series would normally be inconclusive rather than decisive.
